facts.statement: The type species of the genus Miotadorna is Miotadorna sanctibathansi, which was described by Worthy et al. in 2007.
Miotadorna catrionae was synonymized with Miotadorna sanctibathansi by Tennyson et al. in 2022.
Miotadorna is an extinct genus of tadornine ducks that lived in New Zealand during the Miocene epoch.
facts.quote: Miotadorna is a genus of extinct tadornine ducks from the Miocene of New Zealand.

facts.statement: The genus Miotadorna contains two species: M. sanctibathansi and M. catrionae, also known as Catriona's shelduck.
facts.quote: It contains two species, M. sanctibathansi, and M. catrionae (Catriona's shelduck).

facts.statement: M. sanctibathansi was described from a fossilized right humerus found in the Saint Bathans Fauna within the lower Bannockburn Formation of the Manuherikia Group in the Central Otago region of New Zealand's South Island.
facts.quote: M. sanctibathansi was described from a fossilised right humerus collected from the Saint Bathans Fauna, in the lower Bannockburn Formation of the Manuherikia Group, found by the Manuherikia River in the Central Otago region of the South Island.

facts.statement: The genus name Miotadorna indicates that the describers viewed the bird as a Miocene shelduck similar to modern Tadorna.
facts.quote: The genus name reflects the view of the describers that the bird is a Miocene shelduck similar to those in the genus Tadorna.

facts.statement: M. catrionae, described in 2022, is the largest duck species discovered in the St Bathans fossil deposits.
facts.quote: M. catrionae, described and named in 2022, is the largest duck species so far discovered in the St Bathans fossil deposits.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of M. catrionae is a large right humerus.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen is a large right humerus.

facts.statement: M. catrionae is very similar to M. sanctibathansi but is distinguished by its larger size and differing proportions.
facts.quote: It is noted as being very similar to M. sanctibathansi, but its large size and differing proportions distinguish it from that species.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the size difference between M. catrionae and M. sanctibathansi may represent sexual dimorphism, though this explanation is not fully supported by the morphological evidence.
facts.quote: This size difference may represent sexual dimorphism, although the morphological changes are not sufficiently explained by this.

facts.statement: Worthy et al. (2022) considered M. catrionae a synonym of M. sanctibathansi, believing the larger specimen represented a larger sex rather than a distinct species.
facts.quote: Worthy et al., (2022) considered M. catrionae to be a synonym of M. sanctibathansi, as they believed it was more likely that the larger specimen represented a larger sex.

facts.statement: Miotadorna belongs to the subfamily Tadorninae.
Miotadorna is classified within the family Anatidae.
Miotadorna lived between 18.7 and 15.9 million years ago, spanning the Burdigalian to Langhian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Burdigalian to Langhian (18.7 to 15.9 million years ago)
